sources.quality_note: Recent national LeDeR-based data; mortality data only (age at death, not mortality risk); avoidable = death before 75 from OECD preventable/treatable causes.

claims.claim: In the Confidential Inquiry, median age at death of people with intellectual disabilities was 64; men 13 and women 20 years younger than the general population
claims.supporting_passage: the median age at death was 64 years (IQR 52-75). The median age at death of male individuals with intellectual disabilities was 65 years (IQR 54-76), 13 years younger than the median age at death of male individuals in the general population of England and Wales (78 years). The median age at death of female individuals with intellectual disabilities was 63 years (IQR 54-75), 20 years younger than the median age at death for female individuals in the general population (83 years).
claims.pico_timeframe: 247 deaths of people with ID, south-west England, 2010-2012; comparator general population of England and Wales
claims.safe_wording: In an inquiry into 247 deaths in south-west England (2010 to 2012), men with a learning disability died a median of 13 years younger, and women 20 years younger, than the general population.
claims.qualifications: Regional and more than a decade old; name place and years.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Newer national LeDeR data (Yu 2026) show a similar gap.

numbers.meaning: median age at death men with ID vs men general population
median age at death women with ID vs women general population

claims.claim: 37% of deaths amenable to good-quality health care vs 13% in general population
claims.supporting_passage: Avoidable deaths from causes amenable to change by good quality health care were more common in people with intellectual disabilities (37%, 90 of 244) than in the general population of England and Wales (13%).
claims.safe_wording: About 37 in 100 of these deaths were from causes that good health care can usually treat, compared with 13 in 100 in the general population.
claims.qualifications: Use 'amenable to good health care' definition; do not mix with LeDeR 'avoidable'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Definitions of avoidable death differ between studies.

numbers.meaning: deaths amenable to healthcare, ID group

claims.claim: Contributory factors included advance care planning, Mental Capacity Act adherence, adjusting care as needs changed, carers not feeling listened to
claims.supporting_passage: Contributory factors to premature deaths in a subset of people with intellectual disabilities compared with a comparator group of people without intellectual disabilities included problems in advanced care planning (p=0·0003), adherence to the Mental Capacity Act (p=0·0008), living in inappropriate accommodation (p<0·0001), adjusting care as needs changed (p=0·009), and carers not feeling listened to (p=0·006).
claims.safe_wording: Problems found more often included not adjusting care as needs changed and carers not feeling listened to.
claims.qualifications: Subset comparison; judgements by review panels.

claims.claim: Recent national (LeDeR) data on age at death and avoidable deaths
claims.supporting_passage: The median age at death was markedly lower in this group (57.9 years) compared to those with mild or moderate intellectual disability (65.0 years) and the general population (81.9 years) (p < 0.001). We classified two-fifths of deaths among adults with severe or profound intellectual disability as avoidable (39.5%)
claims.pico_timeframe: England, LeDeR and ONS deaths 2021-2023; adults
claims.safe_wording: In England in 2021 to 2023, adults with a mild or moderate learning disability died at a median age of 65 and those with a severe or profound learning disability at 58, compared with 82 in the general population.
claims.qualifications: LeDeR covers deaths reviewed, not all; 39.5% avoidable refers only to severe/profound group, avoidable = before 75 from OECD causes. Not the official LeDeR annual report (not opened).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: LeDeR annual report figures not verified.

numbers.meaning: median age at death, severe/profound ID
median age at death, mild/moderate ID
median age at death, general population
deaths classified avoidable, severe/profound ID only

claims.claim: Learning disability liaison nurses and hospital passports exist and help; liaison nurse input linked with more reasonable adjustments
claims.supporting_passage: One-third of people with intellectual disability who died in hospital in England between 2016 and 2021 had input from an intellectual disability liaison nurse. ... associated with increased likelihood of reasonable adjustments being made to care (adjusted OR (aOR) 1.95, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.32) ... but was not associated with a rating of overall quality of care received (aOR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.12). | the use of the hospital passport and the intellectual disability liaison nurse to significantly improve the hospital experience for adults with intellectual disabilities was identified in two of the studies.
claims.pico_timeframe: Sheehan: adults with ID who died in English hospitals 2016-2021; McCormick: 5 qualitative studies
claims.safe_wording: Only about 1 in 3 people with a learning disability who died in English hospitals (2016 to 2021) had seen a learning disability liaison nurse; when one was involved, care was more often adjusted to the person's needs. People with a learning disability have said hospital passports and liaison nurses made hospital easier.
claims.qualifications: Association only; no difference in overall quality rating; do not convert OR to 'twice as likely'.

numbers.meaning: of those who died in hospital 2016-2021 had liaison nurse input

claims.claim: Equality Act 2010 legal duty of reasonable adjustments
claims.safe_wording: Omit the legal claim, or frame as 'hospitals should make reasonable adjustments' (judgement).
claims.qualifications: Legislation not opened; Equality Act does not apply in Northern Ireland.

claims.claim: Barriers to rapid (compassionate) discharge include getting equipment and medicines and poor communication between teams
claims.supporting_passage: Process mapping, an Ishikawa diagram and a Pareto chart were used to identify barriers, which included timely acquisition of home equipment and medication and poor communication among stakeholders. | Barriers identified included sourcing of equipment, communication between teams and clunky paperwork.
claims.pico_timeframe: Single-hospital QI projects, Singapore and Somerset England, 2020-2023
claims.safe_wording: Hospital improvement projects in England and Singapore found the usual hold-ups were getting equipment and medicines to the home, poor communication between teams, and paperwork.
claims.qualifications: Two single-site QI projects; 'main' barrier ranking not claimed.

claims.claim: Some people referred for rapid discharge die in hospital before discharge
claims.supporting_passage: The average time to discharge was 6.3 days and 29% died in hospital, as median survival was only 15 days. ... In phase 2, we extended the pilot, and 104 patients were identified; 94 people were discharged to home, with a median of wait of 1 day (range 0-7) to discharge, and 10 (9.6%) died prior to discharge (median 1 day; range 0-4). Median survival from discharge for the 94 who achieved their wishes to go home to die was 9 days
claims.pico_timeframe: Somerset DGH patients wishing to die at home, referred to end-of-life discharge team; pilot to 2023
claims.safe_wording: In one English hospital, before a faster process, 29 in 100 people waiting to go home to die died in hospital first; after the team sped things up to a median wait of 1 day, about 10 in 100 still died before they could leave.
claims.qualifications: Single hospital, uncontrolled before/after; baseline from earlier work; 29% not strictly comparable population.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Alias 2024 reports failures from clinical deterioration or delays in home oxygen.

numbers.meaning: died in hospital, earlier work, average discharge time 6.3 days

claims.claim: NICE NG31 covers anticipatory prescribing for last days of life
claims.supporting_passage: This Concise Guideline overviews NICE Clinical Guideline (NG31), which addresses: recognising dying; communication and shared decision making; maintaining hydration; and pharmacological symptom control, including anticipatory prescribing.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in last days of life
claims.safe_wording: National guidance on care in the last days of life includes planning medicines in advance for symptoms that may come.
claims.qualifications: Recommendation text not opened; keep general. NICE is England-focused.

claims.claim: NHS CHC Fast Track funds care quickly (England)
claims.supporting_passage: assessment processes for care funding, through continuing healthcare fast-track funding often inhibit people being able to die at home.
claims.safe_wording: Leave Fast Track out, or say only that in England waiting for care funding assessment can hold up going home to die.

candidates.reason: Heslop figures and contributory factors supported; recent LeDeR-based data (Yu 2026) and liaison nurse data (Sheehan 2024) found; Equality Act legal duty not opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Use Heslop 2014 (south-west England, 2010-12) for the sex gap and 37 vs 13 in 100; add 2021-23 England median ages (65 mild/moderate, 58 severe/profound vs 82); note only 1 in 3 who died in hospital saw a liaison nurse. Frame reasonable adjustments as what hospitals should do, without citing the Act. Do not imply these are mainly old-age deaths.

candidates.reason: Barriers and died-before-discharge claim now sourced (Morrison 2024, English); Fast Track not verified from National Framework.
candidates.revised_angle: Same-day parallel steps for all UK readers; cite equipment, medicines, communication and paperwork as usual hold-ups; one English hospital: 10 in 100 still died before leaving even with a 1-day median wait (29 in 100 before). Omit Fast Track or mention only that funding assessment can delay in England.
